newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: E.Europe share indices fall as floods damp spirits.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe share indices fall as floods damp spirits.

text.p: The Warsaw WIG Index outpaced other regional bourses while fears crept in elsewhere that heavy flooding in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland might dampen spirits in the coming months.
Budapest was the only other gainer as late losses pulled back Bucharest and Bratislava. Czech and Slovenian equities slipped and in Croatia volumes were thin and prices mixed.
PRAGUE

Czech shares edged lower over the course of the week after a sharp rise last Friday, pushed down by concern over the economy, especially after torrential rains left nearly one-third of the country flooded, closing many major factories.

Dealers said data showing another contraction in industrial output in May was more bad news for a market reeling from poor economic fundamentals that have helped turned investor attention to other bourses in the region.

"Heavy flooding in parts of the country could also damage the economy, though it is still early to tell how much, which could hurt fundamentals even further," said Boris Gomez of ING Barings. "At this point, we just have to wait and see."
Added one regional analyst in London: "We are really concerned. Poland, the Czechs, Slovakia, they all may see share prices fall in some sectors because of plant closures."
BUDAPEST
The Budapest BUX index closed lower on Friday as the market's corrective phase, which started on Thursday after six successive record highs, entered its second day.

Traders said the market's recent rally, which bolstered the BUX index by eight percent, justified the downward correction but gave no reason to believe the market's long-term upward trend would come to halt.
But they added they expected a virtually stagnant market in the short-term.

"I think today's fall fully fits in with expectations," said Geza Raner of Bank Austria-Investment Rt. "It's just a cautious decline, there might be a 0.5 percent dip (on Monday) then the market will become flat."
WARSAW

Polish shares rose 1.7 percent this week to 15,832.8 points but analysts predicted a flatter market next week despite Thursday and Friday's high turnover caused by strong demand for copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA.
KGHM rose 2.1 percent to 24 zlotys on Friday.

"The recent growth was likely linked to hopes that money invested in KGHM would return to the market, which has probably happened to a degree, but it seems the extra demand was too short-term and small to lift prices significantly," said Dariusz Szepieniec, an analyst at Bank Slaski brokerage.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) saw another week of listless trading, with brokers expecting the situation to last at least over the summer.
The official 16-share SAX index dropped 0.83 points, or 49 percent, over the week.
"It is quite difficult to predict a stronger trend as the market still remains uncertain and very fragile," said Dusan Sykora of ING Barings.
But he added that, from a longer-term perspective, shares were more likely to rise rather than fall further as the current low prices may make Slovak shares attractive to foreign investors.
BUCHAREST
Romanian shares fell back on Friday with dealers saying the decline was part of an expected correction.
Romania's failure to win inclusion in the first wave of NATO expansion at the Madrid summit was ignored by investors.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks traded mostly lower on dwindling volumes with blue chips Pliva and Zagrebacka Banka absent from the market for the first time in months.
Food processor Podravka was a rare exception in otherwise sluggish trade after agreeing a loan this week.
"The latest rise in the price of Podravka shares is a direct result of a 60 million german mark loan at 2.50 percent over Libor it got on Wednesday," one analyst said.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell 1.36 percent this week, as the blue-chip SBI index dropped 19.94 points to 1,440.2.
But market participants forecast that the index was likely to rise by about 20 percent over the summer with foreign capital flows showing no signs of slowing.
"Over the summer traders will most probably be very busy, much more than we previously expected," said Nena Jarc, a trader at Nova Ljubljanska banka.
But she said some profit-taking was to be expected over the short term.
